library(glmmTMB)
library(dplyr)

  select(
    Survived, Survived.Char, Sex, Sex.Binary,
    Pclass, Pclass.Char, Age
  )

The analysis includes 714 passengers with complete information on survival, sex, age, and ticket class. The mean age was 29.7 years (SD = 14.53), with ages ranging from 0.42 to 80 years. The categorical groups were not evenly distributed: 453 passengers were male and 261 were female. First, second, and third class contained 186, 173, and 355 passengers, respectively. Overall, 290 passengers survived and 424 died. These summaries describe the composition of the complete-case sample. We will examine comparisons of survival between different passenger groups in later analysis. ## Predictions and model specification I expect survival to be associated with sex, ticket class, and age. I predict that female passengers had higher survival odds than male passengers, which is consistent with the possibility that women were prioritized during evacuation. I also expect first-class passengers to have higher survival odds than second- and third-class passengers, potentially due to differences in access to evacuation routes and resources. Finally, I expect younger passengers to have higher survival odds if children were prioritized. ### Four competing models


Code
# Model 0: intercept only
mod0 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ 1,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = titanic
)

# Model 1: sex
mod1 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex.Binary,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = titanic
)

# Model 2: sex and ticket class
mod2 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex.Binary + Pclass,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = titanic
)

# Model 3: sex, ticket class, and age
mod3 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex.Binary + Pclass + Age,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = titanic
)




Interpretation of the intercept
In mod1, the intercept represents the log-odds of survival for male passengers because Sex. Binary is coded 0 for males. In mod2, the intercept represents the log-odds of survival for male passengers in first class, which is the reference ticket category. In mod3, the intercept represents the log-odds of survival for male passengers in first class at age zero. So, the intercept changes meaning as predictors are added. The age-zero intercept provides a mathematical reference point rather than describing a typical passenger. ## Model comparisons ### Nested-model likelihood-ratio tests

Combined model-comparison table


Code
# Extract model-level statistics
model_stats <- bind_rows(
  mod0 = broom.mixed::glance(mod0),
  mod1 = broom.mixed::glance(mod1),
  mod2 = broom.mixed::glance(mod2),
  mod3 = broom.mixed::glance(mod3),
  .id = "Model"
) |>
  select(Model, AIC, BIC, logLik) |>
  mutate(
    deviance = -2 * logLik,
    residual_df = c(
      df.residual(mod0),
      df.residual(mod1),
      df.residual(mod2),
      df.residual(mod3)
    )
  )

# Extract the nested-model test results
nested_tests <- as.data.frame(model_tests) |>
  select(`Chi Df`, Chisq, `Pr(>Chisq)`) |>
  rename(
    nested_df = `Chi Df`,
    nested_chisq = Chisq,
    nested_p = `Pr(>Chisq)`
  )

# Combine results in the same model order
comparison_table <- bind_cols(model_stats, nested_tests)

# Format the table
comparison_table |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Comparison of logistic regression models"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    logLik = "Log-likelihood",
    deviance = "Deviance",
    residual_df = "Residual df",
    nested_df = "Nested df",
    nested_chisq = "Nested chi-square",
    nested_p = "Nested p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(AIC, BIC, logLik, deviance, nested_chisq),
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(residual_df, nested_df),
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  fmt(
    columns = nested_p,
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(
        is.na(x),
        NA_character_,
        ifelse(x < 0.001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x))
      )
    }
  ) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "\u2014")

Interpretation of model comparisons
Model fit improved with each addition of predictors. Adding sex to the null model greatly reduced AIC from 966.52 to 754.70 and BIC from 971.09 to 763.84. The likelihood-ratio test indicated that this improvement was statistically significant with chi-square(1) = 213.82, p < .001. Adding ticket class further improved fit, chi-square(2) = 78.27, p < .001, reducing AIC to 680.43 and BIC to 698.71. Adding age produced an additional significant improvement, chi-square(1) = 25.15, p < .001. Model 3 had the lowest AIC (657.28) and BIC (680.14) among the four candidate models. So, both information criteria and the likelihood-ratio tests support retaining all three predictors at this stage. Although AIC and BIC penalize additional model complexity, the improvements in fit outweighed these penalties. Model 3 is therefore the leading candidate, subject to diagnostic assessment. ## Diagnostics Model 3 was selected for initial diagnostic assessment because it had the lowest AIC and BIC, and each addition of predictors significantly improved model fit.


Simulated residual diagnostics


Code
res_mod3 <- DHARMa::simulateResiduals(
  fittedModel = mod3,
  n = 1000,
  seed = 123
)

plot(res_mod3, quantreg = FALSE)











Residual patterns across age


Code
DHARMa::plotResiduals(
  res_mod3,
  form = titanic$Age,
  quantreg = FALSE,
  rank = FALSE,
  xlab = "Age (years)"
)









The residual-versus-age plot showed a smooth curve close to 0.5 across most of the adult age range, with departures among the youngest and oldest passengers. These patterns suggest that a single linear age term on the log-odds scale may not fully capture the age–survival relationship. The upward curve at the oldest ages should be interpreted cautiously since relatively few observations occur in that range. This visual diagnostic does not establish statistically significant nonlinearity, but it identifies a limitation of the specified model. ### Collinearity


Code

collinearity_results

The collinearity assessment indicated little overlap among predictors that would inflate coefficient uncertainty. VIF values were 1.07 for sex, 1.42 for ticket class, and 1.33 for age. These results suggest that problematic multicollinearity is not evident in this model. ### Complete or quasi-complete separation

separation_check <- glm(
  Survived ~ Sex.Binary + Pclass + Age,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = titanic,
  method = detectseparation::detect_separation

A formal separation check using the same predictors as Model 3 detected no complete separation and no quasi-complete separation. The check indicated that finite maximum-likelihood estimates exist for all coefficients. Separation therefore does not appear to be a problem for this model. ### Events per predictor coefficient


Code
n_survived <- sum(titanic$Survived == 1)
n_died <- sum(titanic$Survived == 0)

# Exclude the intercept from the coefficient count
n_predictor_coefficients <- length(
  fixef(mod3)$cond
) - 1

events_per_coefficient <- min(
  n_survived,
  n_died
) / n_predictor_coefficients

events_summary <- data.frame(
  Survived = n_survived,
  Died = n_died,
  Predictor_coefficients = n_predictor_coefficients,
  Events_per_coefficient = events_per_coefficient
)

events_summary |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Outcome counts and events per coefficient"

    Predictor_coefficients = "Predictor coefficients",

  Survived ~ Sex.Binary + Pclass + Age,

# Compare predictor coefficients and odds ratios
influence_comparison <- data.frame(
  Predictor = names(fixef(mod3)$cond),
  Original_coefficient = unname(fixef(mod3)$cond),
  Sensitivity_coefficient = unname(
    fixef(mod3_sensitivity)$cond

) |>
  mutate(
    Original_OR = exp(Original_coefficient),
    Sensitivity_OR = exp(Sensitivity_coefficient)

  filter(Predictor != "(Intercept)")

Cook’s distance identified 47 observations above the screening threshold of 4/n (approximately 0.00560), with a maximum Cook’s distance of 0.02905. These observations were treated as cases for investigation instead of being automatically removed. A sensitivity analysis removing the passenger with the largest Cook’s distance preserved the direction of every predictor coefficient. The odds ratio for sex changed from 12.463 to 12.936. The second- and third-class odds ratios changed from 0.270 to 0.253 and from 0.076 to 0.069, respectively. The age odds ratio changed from 0.964 to 0.961. So, the broad pattern of associations was not driven by this single observation. ### Summary of diagnostic findings
Model 3 converged successfully and had a positive-definite Hessian. The collinearity check indicated low VIF values, and the formal separation check detected no complete separation and no quasi-complete separation. There were 72.50 observations in the smaller outcome group per predictor coefficient, providing a reassuring events-per-coefficient ratio without guaranteeing model adequacy. The DHARMa uniformity test did not detect an overall departure from the expected residual distribution (p = .512), and the outlier test was not statistically significant at the .05 level (p = .057). A numerical warning arose when fitting the diagnostic quantile curves. So, the plots were regenerated using a smooth curve instead, without changing the logistic model. These revised curves were used for visual assessment rather than formal quantile testing. Influence screening flagged observations for investigation, but removing the single most influential passenger did not change the directions of the estimated associations. Overall, Model 3 remains the preferred candidate among the four prescribed models, but the residual-versus-age plot suggests possible inadequacy of its linear age term, particularly at the age extremes. The age coefficient reflects the model’s assumption that each additional year of age changes the log-odds of survival by the same amount. Importantly, it does not confirm that this relationship holds across all ages. Exploring more flexible ways to model age would be a useful next step beyond the four models considered here. ## Preferred model and interpretation ### Model selection
I selected Model 3, which includes sex, ticket class, and age, as the most defensible model among the four candidates. The nested-model likelihood-ratio tests showed that each successive addition improved model fit, and Model 3 had the lowest AIC and BIC. Although this model includes more predictor coefficients than the alternatives, the improvement in fit supports keeping all three predictors. Diagnostic checks showed successful convergence, low collinearity, and no detected separation. Removing the single most influential observation also left the direction and broad interpretation of the estimated associations unchanged. However, the residual-versus-age plot suggested that the linear age term may not fully capture the relationship across all ages. Model 3 therefore provides the best-supported balance of fit, complexity, and interpretability among the prescribed models, allowing the association between each passenger characteristic and survival to be examined while holding the other included characteristics constant.


Code
preferred_model <- mod3




Coefficient estimates


Code
# Extract coefficients and 95% confidence intervals
coef_results <- broom.mixed::tidy(
  preferred_model,
  effects = "fixed",
  component = "cond",
  conf.int = TRUE,
  conf.level = 0.95,
  conf.method = "Wald",
  exponentiate = FALSE
)

# Store odds ratios for the written interpretations later
coef_results <- coef_results |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    odds_ratio = exp(estimate),
    or_low = exp(conf.low),
    or_high = exp(conf.high)
  )

# Prepare and display the coefficient table
coef_results |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    predictor = dplyr::recode(
      term,
      "(Intercept)" = "Intercept",
      "Sex.Binary" = "Female (vs. male)",
      "Pclass2" = "Second class (vs. first class)",
      "Pclass3" = "Third class (vs. first class)",
      "Age" = "Age (per additional year)"
    ),
    confidence_interval = sprintf(
      "[%.3f, %.3f]", conf.low, conf.high
    ),
    p_value = dplyr::if_else(
      p.value < 0.001,
      "< .001",
      sprintf("%.3f", p.value)
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    predictor,
    estimate,
    std.error,
    confidence_interval,
    p_value
  ) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Preferred Model: Logistic Regression Coefficients",
    subtitle = "Outcome: survival; coefficients on the log-odds scale"
  ) |>
  gt::cols_label(
    predictor = "Predictor",
    estimate = "Coefficient",
    std.error = "Standard error",
    confidence_interval = "95% CI",
    p_value = "p-value"
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = c(estimate, std.error),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  gt::tab_source_note(
    source_note = paste(
      "Reference categories: male and first class.",
      "Confidence intervals use the Wald method."
    )
  )

Interpretation of coefficients


Code
# Retrieve and format a numerical value from the tidy results
coef_value <- function(term_name, column_name, digits = 3) {
  value <- coef_results |>
    dplyr::filter(term == term_name) |>
    dplyr::pull(dplyr::all_of(column_name))

  sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), value)
}


Holding ticket class and age constant, female passengers had log-odds of survival that were 2.523 higher than those of male passengers. Their odds of survival were 12.463 times those of male passengers (95% CI: 8.300 to 18.714). Holding sex and age constant, second-class passengers had a log-odds difference of -1.310 compared with first-class passengers, corresponding to odds of survival that were 0.270 times those of first-class passengers (95% CI: 0.156 to 0.465). Third-class passengers had a corresponding log-odds difference of -2.581, with odds of survival that were 0.076 times those of first-class passengers (95% CI: 0.044 to 0.131), holding sex and age constant. Finally, holding sex and ticket class constant, each additional year of age was associated with a change of -0.037 in the log-odds of survival. The corresponding odds ratio was 0.964 per year (95% CI: 0.949 to 0.978), indicating lower survival odds with increasing age under the model’s constant age-slope assumption.
The intercept of 1.254 represents the estimated log-odds of survival for a male passenger in first class at age zero. Converting the intercept from log-odds to odds gives baseline survival odds of 3.505. These odds apply to a male passenger in first class at age zero, rather than comparing two passenger groups. Because age was not centered, this reference profile does not represent a typical passenger. ### Overall model performance


Code
# Extract overall fit statistics
model_performance <- broom.mixed::glance(preferred_model)

# Compare the preferred model with the intercept-only model
overall_chisq <- 2 * (
  as.numeric(logLik(preferred_model)) -
    as.numeric(logLik(mod0))
)

overall_df <- attr(logLik(preferred_model), "df") -
  attr(logLik(mod0), "df")

overall_p <- pchisq(
  overall_chisq,
  df = overall_df,
  lower.tail = FALSE
)

# Assemble and display the performance table
performance_table <- data.frame(
  Statistic = c(
    "Number of passengers",
    "Estimated coefficients (including intercept)",
    "Log-likelihood",
    "AIC",
    "BIC",
    "Overall likelihood-ratio chi-square",
    "Likelihood-ratio degrees of freedom",
    "Likelihood-ratio p-value"
  ),
  Value = c(
    as.character(nobs(preferred_model)),
    as.character(nrow(coef_results)),
    sprintf("%.2f", model_performance$logLik),
    sprintf("%.2f", model_performance$AIC),
    sprintf("%.2f", model_performance$BIC),
    sprintf("%.2f", overall_chisq),
    as.character(overall_df),
    ifelse(
      overall_p < 0.001,
      "< .001",
      sprintf("%.3f", overall_p)
    )
  )
)

performance_table |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Overall Performance of the Preferred Model",
    subtitle = "Survival predicted by sex, ticket class, and age"
  ) |>
  gt::tab_source_note(
    source_note = paste(
      "The overall likelihood-ratio test compares the preferred",
      "model with the intercept-only model using the same passengers."
    )
  )

Summary of findings
I compared four nested binary logistic regression models to examine how sex, ticket class, and age were associated with survival on the Titanic among 714 passengers with complete data. Model 3, which included all three predictors, was selected because the model comparisons supported its improved fit and the diagnostic checks were generally reassuring. It also fit better than the intercept-only model (likelihood-ratio chi-square = 317.23, df = 4, p < .001). In the preferred model, female passengers had 12.463 times the odds of survival of male passengers, holding ticket class and age constant. Second- and third-class passengers had 0.270 and 0.076 times the odds of survival of first-class passengers, respectively, holding sex and age constant. Each additional year of age was associated with an odds ratio of 0.964, holding sex and ticket class constant. Together, these findings indicate that survival was associated with sex, ticket class, and age, with higher survival odds among female passengers, first-class passengers, and younger passengers. Importantly, these results do not describe causal effects. Instead, they describe adjusted associations, and the age finding should be interpreted cautiously because the diagnostic plot suggested that a constant age slope may not fully capture the relationship across all ages. ## Predicted probabilities

title: Titanic Survival Analysis
text:
Discussion and limitations
The results suggest that sex, ticket class, and age were all associated with survival on the Titanic. Female passengers had substantially higher adjusted survival odds than male passengers, while second- and third-class passengers had lower adjusted survival odds than first-class passengers. Older age was also associated with lower survival odds after accounting for sex and ticket class. Together, these findings suggest that survival outcomes differed across demographic and socioeconomic groups.
Sex and ticket class showed substantial differences between groups, whereas the age odds ratio described a smaller change for each additional year. However, these odds ratios should not be directly ranked as measures of predictor importance. Sex and ticket class represent group comparisons, while age is measured in single years. Each predictor improved the model’s fit when it was added in the order used in this analysis of likelihood-ratio tests, but they do not establish which predictor would contribute most regardless of that order. The analysis therefore supports the relevance of all three predictors without providing a definitive ranking of their relative importance.
Several limitations should be considered. The analysis used only passengers with complete information on the included variables, so the findings may not fully represent passengers excluded because of missing data. Ticket class provides some indication of socioeconomic status, but it does not fully reflect a passenger’s financial resources or personal circumstances. In addition, the model did not include other potentially relevant passenger characteristics or interactions, so it cannot establish why the observed survival differences occurred. These results should therefore be interpreted as adjusted associations rather than causal effects.
The model also assumed that each additional year of age had the same association with the log-odds of survival. The residual-versus-age plot suggested that this assumption might not fully capture the relationship at the youngest and oldest ages, although the plot alone does not establish nonlinearity. Influence screening identified many observations for further examination. Removing the single most influential observation did not change the broad findings, but this check did not assess the combined influence of all flagged observations. Future analyses could explore more flexible age specifications, interactions, and additional predictors while checking whether the findings remain stable.

Holding ticket class and age constant, female passengers had log-odds of survival that were 2.523 higher than those of male passengers. Their odds of survival were 12.463 times those of male passengers (95% CI: 8.300 to 18.714). Holding sex and age constant, second-class passengers had a log-odds difference of -1.310 compared with first-class passengers, corresponding to odds of survival that were 0.270 times those of first-class passengers (95% CI: 0.156 to 0.465). Third-class passengers had a corresponding log-odds difference of -2.581, with odds of survival that were 0.076 times those of first-class passengers (95% CI: 0.044 to 0.131), holding sex and age constant. Finally, holding sex and ticket class constant, each additional year of age was associated with a change of -0.037 in the log-odds of survival. The corresponding odds ratio was 0.964 per year (95% CI: 0.949 to 0.978), indicating lower survival odds with increasing age under the model’s constant age-slope assumption.
The intercept of 1.254 represents the estimated log-odds of survival for a male passenger in first class at age zero. Converting the intercept from log-odds to odds gives baseline survival odds of 3.505. These odds apply to a male passenger in first class at age zero, rather than comparing two passenger groups. Because age was not centered, this reference profile does not represent a typical passenger. ## Predicted probabilities
